2611.10129.abstract: The deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio (D/H) has provided key insights into the origin and evolution of the Solar System. Using the James Webb Space Telescope, we detected deuterated methane at $48\sigma$ in a mature giant exoplanet, $\epsilon$ Ind Ab. We measure the planet's D/H ratio to be $(4.4 \pm 0.7) \times 10^{-5}$, which is similar to those of Uranus and Neptune but about twice those of Jupiter, Saturn, and the protosolar nebula. $\epsilon$ Ind Ab's heavy elements (C, O, N, and S) are uniformly enriched to a level similar to Jupiter's. These measurements require $\epsilon$ Ind Ab to have accreted solids with $\mathrm{D/H} \gtrsim 1\%$, at least 30 times more deuterium-rich than typical Solar System comets. Such D/H values are found in the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS and in organic molecules in star-forming regions, indicating that $\epsilon$ Ind Ab accreted pristine solids formed in a very cold environment.

2611.10275.abstract: The near-Earth asteroid 1998 KY26, the target of the Hayabusa2# extended mission, has been proposed as a dark comet that may host volatiles, particularly water, owing to an anomalous out-of-plane nongravitational acceleration that may result from outgassing. This asteroid, however, may also belong to a largely anhydrous taxonomic group. Whether outgassing-driven acceleration is possible strongly depends on how the asteroid stores volatiles in its interior and releases them upon heating at the surface. Thus far, the contentious topic of the existence of volatiles on 1998 KY26 that can cause outgassing has not been extensively examined from a thermophysical standpoint. Here, we show that all locations on the surface or in the interior of 1998 KY26 have orbit-averaged temperatures significantly above the sublimation point of volatiles in vacuum. Across 13 thermal characterizations, this observation is found to be consistent despite parameter variations in equivalent diameter, thermal conductivity, Bond albedo, specific heat capacity, and spin pole ecliptic latitude and longitude. Our temperature model results indicate that the water outgassing rate on 1998 KY26 would be too high to maintain buried ice, refining the understanding of the asteroid's composition.

2611.10342.abstract: Detection and characterization of Earth-like worlds is a primary science goal for the upcoming NASA flagship Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO). The HWO mission will be the first of its kind to specifically search for Earth-like worlds around Sun-like stars and characterize their atmospheres to identify potential biosignatures. A mission with such ambitious science goals thus requires equally robust and physically realistic simulation tools. In this work, we extend the realism of the EXOSIMS framework by incorporating phase-dependent biosignature detectability. We use the spectral retrieval tool rfast to determine the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) required to detect atmospheric O2 and H2O as a function of planetary phase and incorporate these requirements directly into EXOSIMS characterization integration-time calculations. Although the required molecular detection SNR decreases toward increasingly crescent phases, successful molecular detections are concentrated at intermediate phase angles, demonstrating the competing effects of molecular information content and direct-imaging observability. Relative to fixed characterization thresholds of SNR = 5 for H2O and SNR = 8.5 for O2, the phase-dependent treatment increases mean molecular detection yield by 76.8 percent for H2O and 29.7 percent for O2. Ultimately, we provide a framework that improves simulation fidelity, increases the realism of EXOSIMS as we expand to assess additional biosignatures in future work, and marries detection and characterization in yield modeling as we look to the future with HWO.

2611.12158.abstract: Millimetre-to-centimetre orbital debris poses a hazard to spacecraft, but its abundance remains difficult to measure. Spaceborne radars offer a substantial sensitivity advantage at close range: received echo power decreases with the fourth power of distance, so an otherwise identical object ten times closer produces a 10,000 times stronger echo. We investigate this opportunity using openly available Sentinel-1 radar voltages recorded on six calendar days. Catalogue-assisted processing identifies a manually validated sample of 76 objects at ranges of 41.7--492.9 km, including satellites, rocket bodies and debris fragments. A blind search recovers two selected debris transits without using their orbital predictions during detection. A short debris encounter also demonstrates how precise range and Doppler measurements can refine a catalogue orbit. Ground scatter increases the effective background and is the principal sensitivity limitation in Earth-looking observations. An ideal receiver-noise sensitivity comparison predicts detectable conducting-sphere diameters of approximately 3.4 mm for Sentinel-1 and 0.6 mm for EarthCARE at 10 km range, assuming coherent integration limited by beam transit time and a 10 ms cap. These results establish the feasibility of space-object detection using existing Earth-observation radars and motivate statistical debris surveys and targeted orbit refinement following collision warnings. Observations directed away from Earth and receive windows adapted to nearby objects could improve sensitivity to small debris.

2611.12504.abstract: GQ Lup B is a massive (10-40 M$_{\text{Jup}}$) companion orbiting the young T-Tauri star GQ Lup A at a projected distance of $\sim$110 au (0.7''). It is outside the circumprimary disk in the submm continuum, but its ${\sim}\,63^\circ$ inclined orbit intersects the primary's gas disk twice per period. We report a 5.8$\sigma$ detection of continuum emission at the location of GQ Lup B, obtained with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) at 0.89 mm (band 7). We associate this emission with a dusty disk around the companion, already detected by VLT/NACO and JWST/MIRI in the mid-Infrared. To date, this is the third disk observed at mm wavelengths around a companion spanning the brown dwarf and planetary mass regimes, following PDS 70 c, a gas giant embedded in the parent circumstellar disk, and SR 12 c, a planetary-mass companion at 1200 au from the primary. We retrieve a point source with peak intensity $54.5\pm9.4\,\mu\rm Jy\, beam^{-1}$, co-spatial with GRAVITY astrometry. The emission is spatially unresolved, placing an upper limit on the source radius of 2.3 au (from a synthesized beam of $\sim\,29\times25$ mas). For comparison, this is smaller than 1/3 of the Hill's radius (3-5 au for GQ Lup B, depending on the assumed mass), the theoretical upper limit for circum-planetary disks. Assuming optically thin thermal emission from mm-size grains in a disk-like structure, we infer a mass of 0.0032 M$_\oplus$, while the optically thick limit yields an emission radius of 0.2 au. Assuming a gas to dust ratio of 100, our results indicate a very low disk mass to accretion rate ratio, of the order of $\sim10^4$ years, analogously to the highest accretors in the stellar mass regime. In the case of GQ Lup B, this can be explained by its periodic crossings of the circumprimary disk, which could deliver a substantial amount of gas to the companion's disk over a long timescale.

2611.12540.abstract: The existing {Ö}pik-type collision frequency framework that accounts for the projectile's Lidov-Kozai (LK) secular evolution holds the target's semimajor axis, eccentricity, and inclination fixed and prescribes uniform precession of its longitude of the ascending node and argument of periapsis. This treatment is not readily applicable when the target's eccentricity, inclination, or orbital precession rates undergo appreciable secular variations. Here, we extend the framework of Liang and Liu (2026, arXiv:2608.30972) to address one such case, in which both the projectile and target undergo LK evolution. Using a doubly averaged quadrupole model to describe the secular dynamics of both bodies, we include the target's orbital evolution when evaluating the collision contribution of each orbital intersection configuration. In the numerical example considered, the projectile survival curve predicted using the calculated collision frequency shows an overall decay trend close to that obtained from direct N-body simulations using REBOUND. In addition, we examine whether the long-term mean collision frequency depends on initial states while holding both bodies' semimajor axes, Kozai constants and closed Hamiltonian level curves fixed. Our theoretical analysis indicates that this frequency is independent of initial states when the parameters describing their relative state are jointly equidistributed at the start of successive projectile LK cycles. Numerical cases with different initial states support this conclusion.

2611.12543.abstract: Recent high-resolution molecular line observations of protoplanetary discs have revealed large-scale non-Keplerian features in the gas kinematics of several systems, which can be interpreted as signatures of warps in the disc. Warps can arise from a range of physical mechanisms, and it remains unclear whether the observed kinematic residuals can be uniquely attributed to warping, or to different competing effects. Stellar flybys are one such mechanism capable of both warping a disc and directly perturbing its kinematics. Using 3D smoothed particle hydrodynamics simulations, we study the evolution of protoplanetary discs perturbed by inclined and coplanar stellar flybys, focusing on timescales of several thousand years after periastron rather than the immediate aftermath of the encounter. We find that inclined stellar flybys initially induce warping and twisting in the disc, but that this geometric perturbation is damped on a timescale set by the disc viscosity. Despite this geometric damping, synthetic ALMA observations of the CO kinematics show that complex non-Keplerian spiral features persist in the velocity residuals long after the warped morphology has relaxed, including in coplanar encounters where no warp is ever induced. Fitting these residuals with a simple warped-disc model, the degree of warping in the disc is systematically overestimated. We therefore conclude that kinematic residuals alone are insufficient to establish that a disc is warped, as flybys induce kinematic complexity independently of warps. We further show that scattered light observations provide an independent diagnostic, showing spiral arms and lateral asymmetries.

2611.12560.abstract: The Neptunian ridge has been reported as an overdensity of planets with radii of $\simeq$5-8 R$_\oplus$ and orbital periods of $\simeq$3-6 d, located between the Neptunian desert and the savanna. It was first identified in Kepler data and has recently been reanalysed using our TESS occurrence rates, where it appears as an approximately twofold excess relative to neighbouring regions. We show that the reported excess arises from expressing the occurrence density per unit period, $\mathrm{d}N/\mathrm{d}P$, rather than per unit logarithmic period, $\mathrm{d}N/\mathrm{d}\ln P$, where the logarithmic form is standard in planet demographics. Because the savanna interval used for comparison is twice as wide in period as the ridge, a population uniform in $\ln P$ naturally produces a factor-of-two contrast in $\mathrm{d}N/\mathrm{d}P$. When expressed per unit $\ln P$, the published TESS and Kepler ridge-to-savanna contrasts decrease from 1.6-2.2 to 0.8-1.2, all consistent with unity. A simulated population with a desert but no intrinsic excess reproduces the appearance of a ridge in $\mathrm{d}N/\mathrm{d}P$ precisely. Reanalysing the TESS-SPOC occurrence rates of 5.5-8.5 R$_\oplus$ planets around FGK stars, we find a ridge-to-savanna ratio of $0.91^{+0.21}_{-0.16}$ per unit $\ln P$, which does not support the claimed overdensity at the ridge. Taken together, these tests imply that the published ridge is a result of the scale choice used, rather than a definitive property of the observed planet population.

2611.12581.abstract: Previous work found a higher bulk iron-to-silicon (Fe/Si) ratio in rocky exoplanets relative to their host star, traditionally explained by iron enrichment. An alternative explanation is devolatilization of the planetary abundance ratios with respect to the host star, where volatile elements such as O and S are progressively depleted compared to refractory elements such as Fe and Mg, as in Earth. We explore whether these elemental molar ratios are consistent with a devolatilization trend. We revisit the core mass fraction of 14 rocky exoplanets with masses between 0.5 and 10 Earth masses whose host stars have spectroscopic abundances of Fe, Si, Mg, O, and S in the literature. We use interior structure retrievals with two independent forward models, the Marseille Super-Earth Interior model and pyExoInt, to estimate compositional parameters, including elemental molar ratios, from mass and radius measurements. We find that 8 out of 14 exoplanets in our sample present an Earth-like devolatilization trend, while only one planet shows a 1:1 relationship between planetary and stellar abundances. This suggests that devolatilization offers a plausible explanation for the observed non-1:1 relation. The two interior models agree on the devolatilization trend, demonstrating that our derived trends are robust. The main limiting factor in constraining refractory compositions of rocky planets relative to their host star is the small sample with constrained stellar abundances and the lack of variety in orbital distances. The PLATO mission will help by extending the sample of characterized rocky planets to orbital periods of up to one year. The variety in refractory elemental ratio trends may indicate a wide diversity in bulk composition, outgassing and other mantle properties relevant for habitability.

2611.12637.abstract: We present results of a multi-wavelength extended monitoring campaign of dynamically new long-period comet C/2013 US$_{10}$ (Catalina), captured with the Ultraviolet and Optical Telescope (UVOT) on board the Swift spacecraft covering 5.8 AU inbound to 5 AU outbound. The pipeline and methodology developed for these results is introduced, along with derived water production rates, active areas, and dust content proxy $A(\theta)f\rho$. We describe a Bayesian solution to address the unknown spectral gradient $S'$ of the dust of C/2013 US$_{10}$ necessary for our continuum subtraction calculations. The comet exhibited significant hyperactivity, with the water production rate approaching $2.5 \times 10^{29}$/s and a greatly elevated active area pre-perihelion, settling to approximately 50 km$^2$ post-perihelion. We also report and quantify a near-nucleus UV excess beyond vectorial model predictions, a feature we have dubbed the Pale Blue Spot (PBS), and cover possible candidate species responsible. When interpreted as OH (A-X) band fluorescence, the PBS may point to a secondary release mechanism producing slow-moving hydroxyl radicals that is active even beyond the water snow line.

2611.12655.abstract: Young protoplanetary disks have received increasing attention in recent years, due to observations revealing the presence of substructures in disks younger than one million years, suggesting that planet formation may begin earlier than previously thought. Other recent observations have provided new insights into the evolution of gas and dust in these early stages, enabling comparisons with evolved Class II disks. Yet the physical processes governing the earliest stages of disk evolution remain poorly understood. In this paper, we present two-dimensional thin-disk hydrodynamical simulations of the formation and early evolution of protoplanetary disks, under the influence of self-gravity and turbulent viscosity alone. We explore various properties of disks forming from the collapse of clouds with a range of initial masses and we compare our results with surveys of protoplanetary disks across multiple evolutionary stages. Our simulations broadly reproduce key observational constraints, including the mm fluxes of Class 0 disks and the dust disk radii of later stages. However, our models do not explain the observed gas and dust disk masses of Class I and II disks: while they account for the most massive observed disks, they fail to reproduce the least massive ones. We discuss that simulations incorporating the influence of the star-forming environment might be needed to resolve this discrepancy.

2611.12787.abstract: We present MarsNet, a machine-learned model of the Martian atmosphere trained only on observations. Existing reanalyses assimilate spacecraft retrievals into general circulation models (GCMs), so where observations are sparse their fields largely reflect the model. We therefore use extant reanalyses only for evaluation. MarsNet alternates a two-hour forecast with an update that assimilates the observations of each window, and both steps are learned jointly. Because the Martian record is too sparse for an unrestricted network, learning is confined within a fixed physical structure: the state is in physical units, the forecast uses physical tendencies of fixed form and learned strength, and the update is a bounded Kalman update. MarsNet is trained on Mars Years (MY) 24--31 and evaluated on independent observations. On three seasons of MGS radio-occultation temperatures assimilated by no dataset, MarsNet matches or improves on the three reanalyses in the lowest three scale heights, with a near-surface root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 4.2 K against 4.4--5.4 K, but is less accurate aloft. The model's surface pressures are the most accurate of the four products (RMSE 10 Pa against Curiosity in MY32, compared with 20--46 Pa). On withheld Mars Climate Sounder profiles of MY32, its temperatures beat an observed climatology and persistence, including in ten-sol forecasts without new observations, and its stated uncertainty is close to calibrated. Much of the temperature skill is present before training and appears to come from the structure and tables fitted to the observations, while training mainly improves the surface pressures, at some cost to dust. The model cycles stably through nine Mars years, and the influence of each observation can be traced. Its speed makes experiments on the observing record practical, and it offers an independent reference for GCMs and reanalyses.

2611.12819.abstract: To understand the process of planet formation in the Solar System or any other stellar system, we need to comprehend the interaction between forming planets and the protoplanetary disk. This work presents a study of the interaction of the protoplanetary disk with the protoplanet and the following types of orbital migration that can occur, and to verify this interaction, numerical simulations were performed using the magneto-hydrodynamics code FARGO3D. The researchers made five simulations with a 2-Jupiter-mass planet in the protoplanetary disk. The only parameter varied was the initial radial position with the aim of verifying the influence of this parameter on the behavior of planetary migration. As a result of these simulations, we find that the initial radial coordinate is a very significant parameter in how the planet interacts with the gas in the disk and the formation of gas gaps.

2611.12841.abstract: We present uniform posteriors indicating the presence or absence of stellar and planetary companions over a sample of $10^5$ stars in Hipparcos and Gaia. We use the "G23H" catalog to fit a model that incorporates absolute astrometry constraints from Hipparcos, Gaia DR2, and Gaia DR3, as well as Gaia DR3 photometry, excess RV variability, and includes information from the presence or absence of common-proper motion companions. The resulting posteriors can be used directly to detect new companions, to target RV and imaging follow-up observations, and for downstream demographics studies. We highlight example detections of known and new candidate companions and the companion detection rate across the HR diagram. The modelling approach we present is directly applicable to Gaia DR4 epoch astrometry and RVs. All posteriors are provided as a machine-readable catalog and user-accessible website this http URL.

2611.12849.abstract: The Tierras Observatory is a fully robotic 1.3-m telescope at the Fred Lawrence Whipple Observatory in southern Arizona. Tierras achieves sub-part-per-thousand (ppt) photometric precision on two timescales: intra-night, to detect and characterize transits of planets around nearby mid-to-late M dwarfs, and night-to-night across an observing season, to characterize the long-term variability of their host stars. We describe the facility and instrument design, our photometric pipeline, and our on-sky performance. We present the first ground-based light curves with sub-ppt precision over timescales of months. This precision enables a range of exoplanet-related science, including the measurement of host star rotation periods, the detection of long-period transits, and the discovery of additional terrestrial planets in known M dwarf systems.

2611.12881.abstract: Brown dwarfs are rare as close companions to stars compared to planets and stellar companions, a paucity known as the brown dwarf desert. Whether the desert sits at a fixed companion mass or a fixed companion-to-star mass-ratio $q$ has been difficult to test, because microlensing, radial velocities, and direct imaging have sampled comparatively narrow slices of stellar mass and separation. Here we apply a novel joint-modelling method to Hipparcos and Gaia DR2/DR3 astrometry from 63,254 stars to complete this picture with a sample 1-2 orders of magnitude larger than those of previous wide-orbit demographic studies. For the first time, we present a single survey that measures occurrence rates of both planetary and stellar companions on 3--94 yr orbits ($\sim$2--20\,au) across host masses from M dwarfs to B stars. We find that the desert is a mass-ratio feature: companions are strongly depleted at $q\approx2\%$ independent of stellar mass from M to B stars, and a desert at fixed companion mass is excluded. Furthermore, we find a positive trend in occurrence with metallicity below the mass-ratio desert, but a negative trend above. The desert therefore separates two distinct populations, plausibly two formation channels, that each scale with stellar mass: the lightest stellar-like companions of K stars ($\sim13 \, M_{jup}$) are less massive than the heaviest planet-like companions of B stars ($\sim27, M_{jup}$), which continue well beyond the deuterium-burning limit. Mass-ratio, not mass, is therefore the physically meaningful boundary between planets and their stellar-like counterparts.

2611.10374.abstract: We present the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array Band 7 observations of the hyperfine structure of C$^{17}$O (3-2) and the H$^{13}$CO$^{+}$ (4-3) molecular line emissions of the Class 0 protostellar system HH 212 at $\sim$ 44 au spatial resolution. Radiative transfer models interpreted in the framework of non-ideal MHD of the envelope allow us to estimate an envelope mass of $M_{env}\sim0.12\,M_\odot$ and a mass infall rate of $\dot{M}_{env}\sim4.4-5.7\times10^{-6}\,M_\odot\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$, consistent with values reported in the literature. The models also reveal a systematic radial velocity drift between the neutral tracer (C$^{17}$O (3-2)) and the ionized species (H$^{13}$CO$^{+}$ (4-3)) of $0.1-0.3$ km s$^{-1}$, exceeding the spectral resolution of 0.105 km s$^{-1}$ and consistent with possible ambipolar diffusion in the envelope. The ambipolar diffusion fraction, $f_{AD}\sim 0.1-1$, and the Hall parameter, $\beta_{i,H_2}\gg1$, indicate partial ion-neutral decoupling, with non-ideal effects becoming more significant toward the inner regions. In the envelope, our analysis shows that rotational energy decreases from $\sim 50\,\%$ of the gravitational energy at $R_{cen}$ to $\sim 25\,\%$ at $2R_{cen}$ and $\sim4\,\%$ at 1100 au. In contrast, for $B_0=1$ mG, magnetic energy increases from $\sim 0.4\,\%$ of the gravitational energy at $R_{cen}$ to $\sim2.6\,\%$ at $2R_{cen}$ and $\sim20\,\%$ at 1100 au. The drift velocity expected from radial force balance is consistent with the modeled drift velocity within $\sim300-400$ au of the central source but is lower at larger radii. These results are consistent with a scenario in which ambipolar diffusion leads to partial ion-neutral decoupling, allowing neutrals to move faster than ions within the envelope.

2611.10596.abstract: We investigate whether Solar System dynamics can provide independent constraints on the present day cosmological deceleration parameter $q_0$, offering a complementary approach to conventional cosmological probes. By relating cosmic acceleration to a weak Hooke type radial perturbation, we derive bounds using planetary perihelion precession, trans-Neptunian objects, and Oort cloud dynamics. We obtain relatively robust planetary bounds of $|q_0|\lesssim 10^9$, while the outer Solar System yields potentially stronger, albeit more model dependent, constraints approaching $10^5$. Through Monte Carlo uncertainty propagation and sensitivity analyses, we explore the statistical robustness of these estimates and their dependence on orbital measurements. Finally, we demonstrate how future precision astrometry and outer planet missions could improve these limits by several orders of magnitude, establishing Solar System dynamics as a complementary laboratory for probing cosmological acceleration.

2611.11642.abstract: M dwarfs are the most abundant group of stars in the Galaxy and they are expected to host a large number of exoplanets orbiting in the habitable zone. It is believed that stellar winds of M dwarfs can have a substantial effect on these exoplanets and on the observations of these systems. However, a systematic investigation of how the stellar winds of M dwarfs varies on timescales of a few months to years and how this impacts exoplanets around these stars is missing. We aim to investigate how variability of magnetic field properties of M dwarfs affects their stellar winds, which is essential for future studies of star-planet interactions (SPIs) and planetary habitability. Such variability might shed light on whether SPI signatures are going to repeat. We have compiled a total of 18 magnetic field maps for 6 M dwarfs, with masses between 0.1 and 0.6 $M_\odot$, and rotation periods between 2.7 and 175.6 days. We use these maps as input of 3D magnetohydrodynamic stellar wind simulations. We derive the mass-loss rate, the angular momentum-loss rate, and the Alfvén radius. For the stars with confirmed exoplanets (DS Leo, YZ Cet, and GJ 1151) we investigate the variability of stellar wind properties at the orbit. We find mass-loss rates between $1.0\times10^{-14}~M_\odot~{\rm yr^{-1}}$ and $2.3 \times 10^{-13}~M_\odot~{\rm yr^{-1}}$ and angular momentum-loss rates between $4.6 \times 10^{27}~{\rm erg}$ and $4.9 \times 10^{31}~{\rm erg}$. For individual stars the Alfvén radius, mass-loss rate, and angular momentum-loss rate varied with time by up to a factor of 1.5, 3.8, and 7.4 respectively. Our results follow the observational relation between mass-loss rate and X-ray flux. Due to the time-varying Alfvén surface, exoplanets orbiting DS Leo and YZ Cet move in and out of the sub-Alfvénic regime, affecting the nature of star-planet interactions and prospects for their detection.
